title: No-Repeat Garden Beds
story: A community garden is a 9 by 9 grid of plots, split into nine 3 by 3 beds. There are nine kinds of plant, numbered 1 to 9. To stop pests spreading, no kind may appear twice in the same row, column or bed.
The planting plan is partly filled in, with 0 for an unclaimed plot. Check that what is planned so far breaks no rule.
task: Write validPlan(plots). plots is a 9 × 9 grid, plots[r][c] being the plant in row r, column c, or 0 if the plot is empty. Bed boundaries fall after rows 2 and 5 and after columns 2 and 5.

Return true if no plant number (1 to 9) appears twice in any row, column or bed, and false otherwise. Empty plots never break a rule. Only check the planned plots, not whether the empty ones could all be filled.
constraints: plots has exactly 9 rows, each with exactly 9 numbers.

examples.explanation: Each row, column and bed holds each plant at most once. Empty plots are fine.
This is the first plan plus a 2 at row 2, column 0. Row 2 (1, 4, 6) and column 0 (5, 6) are fine, but the top-left bed already has a 2 at row 0, column 1.

hints: Take the plot at row 2, column 0 in the second example. Which three groups of plots decide whether its plant breaks a rule?
Every plot belongs to one row, one column and one bed: 27 groups in all. For each, you ask "have I seen this plant in this group before?"
Can you number the beds 0 to 8 from r and c, the way rows and columns are numbered? Divide each by 3, rounding down, and try a few plots.

Keep 9 sets each for rows, columns and beds, with bed number (r ÷ 3, rounded down) × 3 + (c ÷ 3, rounded down). Visit every plot once and skip zeros. If the plant is already in its row, column or bed set, return false; otherwise add it to all three. Return true at the end.
bruteForce: For every planted plot, scan the rest of its row, column and bed for the same plant.

On 9 × 9 that is about 81 × 24 checks, so speed is fine. The cost is the code: three scanning loops and fiddly bed bounds. On an n × n garden the work also grows like n³. Recording each plant once in its three groups is shorter and faster.

tests.note: nothing planned: zeros must not count as a plant
full garden, conflict at the very last plot
bed conflict between opposite corners of a bed
same plant in different beds: defeats bed number r/3 + c/3
same plant on the diagonal, all different beds
breaks no rule even though row 0 can never be finished
two plots swapped in a full garden: rows fine, columns broken
row conflict across the whole row
column conflict across the whole column

js: for (let i = 0; i < 9; i++) { rows.push(new Set()); cols.push(new Set()); beds.push(new Set()); }

walkthrough: The rule is 27 small duplicate checks, one per row, column and bed. Give each group its own set, visit every plot once, and drop its plant into its three sets.

The tricky part is the bed number. Math.floor(r / 3) (r // 3 in Python) gives the band of rows, 0 to 2; the same with c gives the band of columns. Treat them as the row and column of a 3 × 3 grid of beds: bed = band row × 3 + band column. Plot (4, 7) is in band row 1, band column 2, so bed 1 × 3 + 2 = 5.
Trace the start of the second example, row by row:
• (0, 1) = 2, bed 0. Row 0, column 1 and bed 0 all get a 2.
• Row 1 adds 5, 6, 8, 9, 1, 2 with no repeats. Bed 0 now holds 2, 5, 6.
• (2, 0) = 2, bed 0. Row 2 and column 0 have no 2, but bed 0 does. Return false.
A common slip is r / 3 + c / 3 as the bed number. It puts plots (0, 4) and (4, 0) in the same "bed" 1, though they are in different beds, and flags repeats that are not there.
solution.timeWhy: For an n × n garden every plot is visited once with O(1) set work; here n = 9, so 81 plots.
solution.spaceWhy: The 3n sets hold at most n plants each.
solution.takeaway: When a grid rule talks about rows, columns and blocks, give each group an id (block = floor(r/k) · k + floor(c/k)) and keep one hash set per group. Each cell is then checked against all its groups in one pass.
